title-group.article-title: Inpatient outcomes associated with heart failure among adults hospitalized with breast cancer.

contrib-group.aff: Midland Academic Medical Center, Columbus, OH
Eastgate Cancer Research Network, New York, NY
Southern Clinical Oncology Center, Atlanta, GA

permissions.copyright-statement: © 2026 by American Society of Clinical Oncology

abstract.p: Background: Patients hospitalized with breast cancer frequently have complex medical comorbidities, but the clinical impact of concurrent heart failure is not well defined. We examined inpatient outcomes and resource utilization associated with this complication. Methods: We analyzed the National Inpatient Sample for 2017–2022. Adult hospitalizations with a diagnosis of breast cancer were identified using ICD-10-CM codes and stratified by the presence or absence of heart failure. Weighted national estimates were generated. Multivariable logistic and linear regression models adjusted for age, sex, race, payer, hospital characteristics, metastatic disease, and comorbidity burden. Results: Among an estimated 184,230 hospitalizations for breast cancer, 16,844 included heart failure. Patients with the complication had a median age of 69 years, and 97.8% were female. Mean length of stay was 6.1 versus 4.0 days, and mean hospital charges were $78,210 versus $55,240. After adjustment, heart failure was associated with higher odds of cardiogenic shock (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 12.8), acute respiratory failure (aOR 3.1), and in-hospital mortality (aOR 2.4). Conclusions: Concurrent heart failure identifies a clinically vulnerable subgroup of hospitalized patients with breast cancer and is associated with greater morbidity, mortality, and resource use. Early recognition and coordinated oncologic and medical management may improve inpatient care. Research Sponsor: None.
